title: WOTS+ chain-position grinding: per-query domination probability under base-w-plus-checksum versus constant-sum encoding at reduced w
claim: An adversary holding one WOTS+ signature (chain positions b) forges by grinding message digests until the encoded position vector dominates b elementwise. At reduced parameters (w in {4,16}, len1 in {8,16}) the per-query domination probability under the FIPS 205 base-w-plus-checksum encoding exceeds that under a constant-sum encoding of equal signature length by at least a factor of 2 for the worst-quartile signature, and the gap is predicted exactly by the lattice-point counts of the two encodings. If the measured ratio stays within the A/A band, the encoding choice is security-neutral at equal size and only the size argument of KN-LIT-6265 remains.
mechanism: Domination needs every coordinate of the new vector to be at least the revealed one. The checksum restores this defence only on average: signatures whose message part is near-maximal have a small checksum, and the checksum digits are then easiest to dominate. A constant-sum encoding fixes the total, so a vector dominating b must equal b, making single-signature domination impossible except by digest collision, while two-signature max-vectors behave differently. The difference is a counting fact over integer vectors, computable exactly, and the grinding experiment checks that the hash behaves like the count predicts.
tracked_object: Per-query probability that a fresh digest's encoded chain-position vector dominates a fixed revealed vector, per encoding, as a function of the revealed vector's checksum quantile; plus the same after q = 2,4 signatures (elementwise max).

title: Depth-limited parallel Grover cost tables per FIPS 205 hash role: multi-target preimage cost under MAXDEPTH and processor count
claim: For each FIPS 205 parameter set and each hash role (F, H, T_len, H_msg, PRF), the cost of the best generic quantum multi-target attack depends on the number of exposed targets t, the depth cap D and the processor count P as G = sqrt(2^n / t) total iterations split across P machines, giving total gates ~ 2^n / (t * D) per machine-depth product when D binds. A machine-checked table over D in {2^40, 2^64, 2^96} and t from the transcript exposure counts shows at least one parameter set whose depth-capped quantum margin falls below its category floor by >= 4 bits when t is taken as the full exposed target count; or none does, which is the comfortable-margin outcome.
mechanism: Grover parallelises badly: splitting the search space over P machines saves only sqrt(P) in depth while multiplying width by P. Under a depth cap D the attacker must use P = 2^n/(t D^2) machines, and total cost scales as 2^n/(t D), so multi-target gain t is fully realised in the quantum setting under depth limits. Tweaks and per-key PK.seed limit t to targets sharing one tweak domain; the table must count t per tweak domain, not per transcript, which is exactly where conventions disagree.
tracked_object: A table T[param_set][role][D][t_convention] -> (log2 total gates, log2 qubit-width, log2 depth) with interval bounds from the oracle-cost range.

title: Grafting-tree fault forgery simulated at reduced h and d: faulty signatures needed for a verified universal forgery, by faulted layer
claim: At reduced parameters (h in {8,12}, d in {2,3,4}, w=16, n=16 bytes), a single transient fault in the computation of a non-top-layer subtree root causes the parent WOTS+ key to sign an attacker-useful wrong root; the number of faulty signatures needed until a grafted subtree yields a verified universal forgery is predicted by the WOTS domination count and is at most 8 for faults on layer d-2 at w=16. The number grows with layer height in a way set by how many signatures reuse the parent one-time key, and an implementation that recomputes and compares roots needs zero-false-negative detection to reach parity with the unfaulted scheme.
mechanism: Upper-layer WOTS+ keys sign the same subtree root every time a signature passes through them, so they are used many times by design and expose one fixed chain-position vector. A fault that corrupts the root being signed makes that key sign a second value, granting the elementwise max of two position vectors. Once the attacker can sign an arbitrary root of their own subtree by domination, they graft a fresh subtree and forge for any message. The layer chosen sets how often a faulted signature hits the same parent key and therefore how many faults are needed.

title: Compressed ADRS and shared SHA-256 midstate: exhaustive tweak-injectivity census of SHA2 versus SHAKE over every reachable address
claim: In the SHA2 instantiation the 32-byte ADRS is compressed to 22 bytes and PK.seed is padded to one block so every call shares a precomputed midstate; in SHAKE the full ADRS is absorbed. Over every address a reduced-parameter signer can reach (h in {8,12}, d in {2,4}, k up to 14, a up to 6, len up to 35), the compressed encoding is injective on reachable addresses with zero collisions, but there exist (type, field) combinations whose compressed images coincide with images from other types when unreachable fields are populated; the reachable/unreachable boundary is the whole safety argument and can be checked exhaustively.
mechanism: Domain separation in tweakable hashing is only as good as the injectivity of the tweak encoding over the addresses the signer actually uses. Compression drops high bytes of layer and tree address and keeps type; if a field exceeds its compressed width in some parameter set, two distinct logical calls share a tweak. The shared midstate means the PK.seed block contributes nothing per call, so domain separation rests entirely on the compressed ADRS bytes. An exhaustive census at reduced sizes and an analytic width check at FIPS 205 sizes decide whether any set is near the boundary.
tracked_object: Set of (encoding, reachable address) pairs mapped to encoded tweak bytes; number of collisions and minimum headroom (bits) between field values used and field width, per parameter set.

title: Verification malleability census at reduced n: accepted mutations per signature field, against a planted lax verifier
claim: At reduced n (8 and 12 bytes) with toy h, d, k, a, single-bit and single-field mutations of honest signatures are accepted by a reference-faithful verifier only through hash collisions, with the accepted-mutation rate per field matching 2^{-8n} times the field's collision surface; a strong-unforgeability gap appears only where the verifier ignores bytes (for example trailing bytes or unused auth-path nodes). A census of accepted mutations per field, compared with a planted lax verifier, decides whether any field of an SLH-DSA signature is non-binding.
mechanism: Every signature byte should enter a hash whose output is compared to the public root. Fields that are recomputed rather than compared (FORS secret values, WOTS chain values, auth-path nodes) can be altered only if a hash collision maps the altered input to the same output; at n of 8 bytes that rate is measurable. A field that is parsed but never hashed would be accepted at rate 1, which is a SUF-CMA break independent of the hash. The census therefore separates hash-limited malleability from parsing-limited malleability.

title: Iteration-skip faults on the WOTS+ chain loop release lower chain values: forgery capability per fault versus bit-flip faults

title: Role-dependent quantum oracle cost: reversible SHA-256 and Keccak circuits sized per FIPS 205 role input length
claim: Quantum generic attacks against SLH-DSA roles have very different per-call oracle costs because inputs differ in length: F is one compression call while T_len on a WOTS public key absorbs len*n bytes (35-67 chains). title: Failure boosting for HQC at reduced n: precomputation per ciphertext versus failure-probability gain from grinding the FO message
claim: Under the FO transform the attacker cannot choose r1, r2, e but can grind messages m, keeping those whose derived (r1, r2, e) have high failure likelihood (e.g., high weight overlap structure).
